title: Astrophysics & Cosmology
subject: Astrophysics
summary: Survey of how physics you already know (radiation, thermodynamics, quantum statistics, relativity) explains stars, galaxies, and the history of the universe: from starlight and stellar structure to compact objects, the Friedmann equations, the CMB, nucleosynthesis, dark matter and dark energy, and inflation.

units.title: Stellar observables and radiation
units.summary: How astronomers get distance, luminosity, temperature, and composition from starlight: parallax, magnitudes, Planck's law, and the Boltzmann and Saha equations (the same Boltzmann populations and ionization equilibria a chemist uses in spectroscopy).

lessons.title: Parallax and the magnitude scale
objectives: Compute a stellar distance in parsecs from a parallax angle in arcseconds and convert between parsecs, light-years, and meters.
Explain why the magnitude scale is logarithmic and why a difference of 5 magnitudes is exactly a factor of 100 in flux.
Convert a magnitude difference between two stars into a flux ratio, and back, using m1 - m2 = -2.5 log10(F1/F2).

lessons.title: Distance modulus, absolute magnitude, and luminosity
objectives: Convert between apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude, and distance using the distance modulus m - M = 5 log10(d/10 pc).
Use the inverse-square law F = L/(4 pi d^2) to compare the luminosities of two stars from their flux ratio or magnitude difference.
Combine a parallax distance with a measured flux to determine a star's luminosity.

lessons.title: Planck's law and Wien's displacement law
objectives: Explain how Planck's energy quantization resolves the ultraviolet catastrophe and why the Planck spectrum is cut off at high frequency.
State Planck's law and derive Wien's displacement law by locating the peak of B_lambda(T); recite the numerical constant.
Connect the Planck distribution to thermal lamp sources and thermal radiation in IR/UV spectroscopy.

lessons.title: Stefan-Boltzmann law, stellar radii, and the color index
objectives: Obtain the Stefan-Boltzmann law L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T_eff^4 from the integral of the Planck function and use it to find a star's radius from L and T_eff.
Explain why a cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun (a large radius outweighs a low surface flux).
Explain how the B-V color index tracks temperature and why it is independent of distance.

lessons.title: Spectral lines and Boltzmann excitation
objectives: Compute Balmer-series wavelengths from the Rydberg formula and explain absorption lines as bound-bound transitions.
Apply the Boltzmann equation to find the ratio of populations of two atomic levels at temperature T (the same factor that governs vibrational and electronic populations in molecular spectroscopy).
Explain why Balmer absorption needs atoms in n = 2 and so is weak in the coolest stars even though hydrogen is abundant there.

lessons.title: Saha ionization, spectral classes, and the HR diagram
objectives: Apply the Saha equation as an ionization equilibrium (a gas-phase equilibrium constant) to explain why hydrogen Balmer lines are strongest near 10,000 K, not in the hottest stars.
Order the spectral classes O B A F G K M by temperature and place main-sequence stars, giants, and white dwarfs on the HR diagram using L, T, and R contours.

units.title: Stellar structure
units.summary: A star as a self-gravitating ball of gas in balance: hydrostatic equilibrium, the equation of state (ideal gas, radiation, degeneracy from P7), nuclear energy sources, and energy transport yield the main sequence.

lessons.title: Hydrostatic equilibrium and the central pressure of a star
objectives: Derive the equation of hydrostatic equilibrium dP/dr = -G M_r rho / r^2 by balancing forces on a thin shell, and write mass continuity dM_r/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho.
Estimate the central pressure and temperature of the Sun from scaling arguments with the mean density and mean molecular weight.

lessons.title: The virial theorem and the Kelvin-Helmholtz timescale
objectives: State the virial theorem 2K + U = 0 for a gravitating gas and show that a contracting star heats up while its total energy decreases (negative heat capacity).
Compute the Kelvin-Helmholtz timescale for the Sun and explain why gravitational contraction cannot power it for billions of years.

lessons.title: Gas pressure, mean molecular weight, and radiation pressure
objectives: Write the ideal-gas pressure with mean molecular weight mu and compute mu for fully ionized hydrogen/helium/metals mixtures.
Write radiation pressure P_rad = aT^4/3 and find the temperature and mass regime where it rivals gas pressure.

lessons.title: Electron degeneracy pressure and which pressure dominates
objectives: Derive the scaling of electron degeneracy pressure, P proportional to rho^(5/3) nonrelativistic and rho^(4/3) relativistic, from the Pauli principle and the uncertainty relation (the free-electron gas of a metal).
Decide, for a given (rho, T), whether ideal gas, radiation, or degenerate-electron pressure dominates.

objectives: Compute the energy released in 4 H -> He-4 from the mass defect and the fraction of rest mass converted (about 0.7%), and estimate the Sun's nuclear lifetime.
Explain what sets the lifetime of a star on the main sequence and why massive stars die young.

lessons.title: Quantum tunneling, the Gamow peak, and the pp and CNO cycles
objectives: Explain why fusion needs quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier at about 10^7 K, and describe the Gamow peak as the product of the Boltzmann tail and the tunneling probability (compare an Arrhenius rate).
Describe the pp chain and the CNO cycle and compare their temperature sensitivities (roughly T^4 versus T^16 to T^20).

lessons.title: Radiative and convective transport and the equations of stellar structure
objectives: Distinguish radiative from convective energy transport and state the criterion for convective instability qualitatively.
Write the four equations of stellar structure (mass, hydrostatic equilibrium, energy generation, energy transport) with their boundary conditions.

units.title: Stellar evolution and compact objects
units.summary: From collapsing clouds to the main sequence, giants, white dwarfs, supernovae, neutron stars, and black holes, driven by degeneracy pressure and nuclear fuel exhaustion.

lessons.title: Jeans collapse and pre-main-sequence contraction
objectives: Derive the Jeans criterion for gravitational collapse of an isothermal cloud and estimate the Jeans mass of a molecular cloud.
Describe pre-main-sequence contraction qualitatively and why protostars start on the Hayashi track.

lessons.title: Post-main-sequence evolution and the ages of star clusters
objectives: Trace the evolution of a 1 and a 10 solar-mass star across the HR diagram: main sequence, red giant branch, helium ignition, AGB or core collapse.
Use the main-sequence turnoff of a star cluster to estimate its age.

Derive the mass-radius relation R proportional to M^(-1/3) by balancing gravity against nonrelativistic degeneracy pressure.

Classify supernovae (Type Ia, Ib/c, II) by spectra and progenitor.

objectives: Estimate neutron-star radius (about 10 km) and density from neutron degeneracy and compare with nuclear density.

State when a collapsing remnant becomes a black hole (a mass above the neutron-star maximum, so that no known pressure can stop the collapse).
Explain how stellar-mass black holes are identified in binary systems by measuring the mass of an unseen compact companion.

units.title: Galaxies and the distance ladder
units.summary: The Milky Way and other galaxies as dynamical systems: rotation curves reveal dark matter, and the cosmic distance ladder leads to Hubble's law.

lessons.title: Galaxy types, the Milky Way, and mass from orbital speeds
objectives: Place galaxies on the Hubble sequence and describe the Milky Way's disk, bulge, and halo.
Derive the enclosed-mass relation M(<r) = v^2 r / G for circular orbits and estimate the Milky Way's mass from the Sun's orbital speed and distance.

lessons.title: Flat rotation curves and dark halos
objectives: Show that a Keplerian curve v proportional to r^(-1/2) is expected beyond the visible mass.
Explain what flat observed rotation curves imply about the enclosed mass M(<r) proportional to r and a dark halo with density falling as 1/r^2.
Compare the enclosed mass at large radius with the visible mass of a galaxy.

objectives: Describe the rungs of the distance ladder (parallax, Cepheid period-luminosity, Type Ia supernovae) and how errors propagate.
List independent lines of evidence for dark matter: cluster dynamics, gravitational lensing, and the Bullet Cluster.

units.title: The expanding universe and the Friedmann equations
units.summary: Homogeneous, isotropic expansion described by a scale factor; the Friedmann equation from Newtonian energy conservation and its GR form; model universes and the benchmark Lambda-CDM cosmology.

lessons.title: The cosmological principle and Hubble's law
objectives: State the cosmological principle and what homogeneous and isotropic mean observationally.
Derive Hubble's law v = H0 d from uniform expansion r = a(t) x and identify H = adot/a.
Estimate the Hubble time and Hubble distance from H0 of about 70 km/s/Mpc.

Compute the deceleration parameter q0 = Omega_m/2 - Omega_Lambda and interpret its sign.
Describe the cosmological constant as vacuum energy and state the size of the mismatch with the naive quantum-field estimate.
